raw_response:
I farm in Quzhou County, so I will stay with the crop pattern that fits this place best: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. That is the system I trust. Our county is a grain area, the weather and irrigation habits match it, and at my age I want a plan that is steady, familiar, and not too complicated to manage. I will not spread myself across too many crops. Cotton or vegetables can bring more trouble with labor, timing, and pests. I would rather keep the work simple and make sure the grain is done properly.

Because it is the start of the growing season, my winter wheat is already in the field, so I will manage it through jointing, heading, and grain filling, then harvest it in early summer. After that I will put in summer maize right away so I do not lose moisture or season length. I will use improved seed, not old saved seed, because I want better stand and more stable yield, but I will avoid chasing the highest-input approach. I will keep fertilizer moderate and balanced, with nitrogen as the main driver but not excessive, because water is always a constraint here and too much nitrogen can waste money and create lodging or disease pressure. For tillage, I will use rotary tillage before wheat because it gives me a clean seedbed, and I will use no-tillage for maize after wheat harvest to save time, save labor, and catch the season quickly. I will irrigate wheat more than maize, since wheat in our area depends more on timely water, while maize can use summer rainfall better. I will spray only as needed for the common local problems and keep the number of applications limited. Since no land size was given, I am assuming I manage 10 mu, and I will use the same 10 mu for both crops in rotation.
